title: Prompt engineering, RAG or fine-tuning?
description: Sort each Cairnway requirement by the cheapest way to adapt a foundation model that meets it.

items.text: Answers must use today's prices, and the price list changes every day.
items.why: RAG fetches current documents at question time. A fine-tuned model would be out of date by tomorrow.

items.text: Get the reply formatted as JSON with three fixed fields, starting this afternoon.
items.why: Clear instructions and an example output in the prompt do this with no training and no extra infrastructure.

items.text: Write thousands of product descriptions in Cairnway's distinctive brand voice, with 5,000 approved examples to learn from, after prompting alone fell short.
items.why: A consistent style learned from many labeled examples is what fine-tuning is for, once prompting isn't enough.

items.text: The assistant must cite which policy document each answer came from.
items.why: RAG retrieves passages from your documents, so the answer can point to its source.

items.text: Show the model two example question-and-answer pairs so it copies their format.
items.why: That is few-shot prompting: the examples go in the prompt, and the model doesn't change.

items.text: Answer staff questions from 10,000 internal documents that are updated every week.
items.why: The knowledge is large and changes often, so retrieving it at question time beats baking it into the model.

items.text: Sort support tickets into Cairnway's 40 internal categories more accurately than prompts can, with 20,000 labeled tickets available.
items.why: A specialized task with plenty of labeled examples, where prompting has hit its limit, suits fine-tuning.

items.text: Make the chatbot's tone friendlier for a one-week pilot, at the lowest cost.
items.why: Changing the instructions is the cheapest, fastest lever and is easy to undo.

items.text: Stop the assistant making up stock levels by giving it the current inventory at question time.
items.why: Grounding answers in retrieved, current data reduces hallucinations about facts the model can't know.

items.text: Adapt the model to a narrow task, writing gear-repair instructions, using a training set of 3,000 prompt-and-response pairs.
items.why: Labeled prompt-and-response pairs are exactly what supervised fine-tuning trains on; the task is built into the model's weights.

items.text: Ask the model to think step by step before recommending a sleeping bag for given conditions.
items.why: Chain-of-thought is a prompting technique; it needs no training and no extra data store.

items.text: Answer questions about this season's new products, which the model has never seen, with the catalog kept in S3.
items.why: New facts that live in your documents are best brought in by retrieval rather than by retraining.
